deep.reconstruction:
Folio 15v continues the table begun on 15r, 'Gemeine Brüche in Decimalbrüche verwandelt' (common fractions converted into decimal fractions). The left column gives the denominator N. Each entry is the full repeating period of k/N. Gauss writes the period and then repeats its first few digits, underlined, to show where it closes.

Underlying theory (implicit; this is Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 312-318): for gcd(k,N)=1 the period of k/N has length L = ord_N(10). The period, read as an integer, is k(10^L-1)/N. Multiplying k by 10 cyclically rotates the period. So the coprime residues fall into e = phi(N)/L classes, the cosets of <10> in (Z/N)^*. One period per class suffices.

Row by row (my numerators and cosets):

* N=81 (continued from 15r, where 1/81, 2/81, 4/81 were given). L = ord_81(10) = 9, phi = 54, so e = 6. This page gives the remaining classes 5/81 = .061728395, 7/81 = .086419753 and 8/81 = .098765432. The case 3/81 = 1/27 = .037 was already on 15r.
* N=83. L = 41, e = 2.
  - Class of 1: 10/83 = .12048192771084337349397590361445783132530 (rotation of the period of 1/83), closing '...25301 | 2048...'.
  - Non-residue class: 13/83 = .15662650602409638554216867469879518072289 | 15662.
* N=89. L = 44, e = 2.
  - 10/89 = .11235955056179775280898876404494382022471910 | 11235 (Fibonacci-related 1/89).
  - 12/89 = .13483146067415730337078651685393258426966292 | 13.
* N=97. 10 is a primitive root, L = 96, e = 1. Gauss gives the single period starting at 10/97: 103092783505154639175257731958762886597938144 | 329896907216494845360824742268041237113402061 | 855670 | 1030927.
* N=101. L = 4, e = 25. Each class is {±k, ±10k}, and the period of k/101 is the 4-digit number 99k. Gauss lists 25 periods: 9900 (class of 1), then 99k for k = 11-18, 20, 21, 23-27, 30, 31, 34, 35, 36, 40, 41, 45, 50. The struck '2970' and '3960' are merely rewritten over ink blots.
* N=103. L = 34, e = 3.
  - 100/103 = .9708737864077669902912621359223300.
  - 11/103 = .1067961165048543689320388349514563.
  - 16/103 = .1553398058252427184466019417475728 | 15533.
* N=107. L = 53, e = 2.
  - 100/107 = .93457943925233644859813084112149532710280373831775700 | 93457.
  - Marginal (15): 15/107 = .14018691588785046728971962616822429906542056074766355 | 14018691.
* N=109. 10 is a primitive root, L = 108. One period of 108 digits starting 9174311..., ending ...85321100 | 9174311.
* N=113. 10 is a primitive root, L = 112. Gauss's first copy skips a segment, which he then supplies in brackets with asterisks marking the insertion points. The corrected period is:
  8849557522123893805309734513274336 [2831858407079646017699] 1150 442477876106194690265486725663 [7168141592920353982300] | 88495.
  This totals 34+22+4+30+22 = 112 digits.

Observed convention (my inference, consistent with every row): the non-principal classes begin at the smallest numerator k > N/10 in that class, so the period starts with a nonzero digit.
- 83: 9, 10, 11, 12 are residues; 13 is the first non-residue.
- 89: 12 is the first non-residue at or above 9.
- 107: 11, 12, 13, 14 are residues; 15 is not.
- 103: 11 and 16 represent the two new cosets.
The principal class is likewise written from its first nonzero digit.

Purpose: this is the working draft of the table of decimal periods for denominators below 1000 promised in DA art. 316/318, printed in Werke II.
errors: N=113: in the first copy Gauss skipped 22 digits (2831858407079646017699) after '...4336' and initially also jumped from '...5663' to the restart, omitting '7168141592920353982300'. Both omissions are corrected by his own bracketed insertions; the corrected 112-digit period is right.
N=107: two digits are overwritten/struck ('7102803', '7383177...'); the final reading is correct.
N=89: a premature closing '91' at the end of line 1 is struck and rewritten as '191011235'; correct.
N=101: '2970' and '3960' were rewritten after ink blots; no arithmetic error.
All other periods check: lengths 9, 41, 44, 96, 4, 34, 53, 108, 112 match ord_N(10), and the digits agree with k(10^L-1)/N.

results.what: Full decimal periods of k/N for N=81,83,89,97,101,103,107,109,113, one representative per coset of <10> in (Z/N)^*
results.modern_name: Table of repetends / multiplicative order of 10 (cyclic numbers, full-reptend primes 97, 109, 113)
results.usually_credited_to: Decimal-period tables go back to Wallis, Lambert, J. Bernoulli III and Robertson (1768), and later H. Goodwyn (1818-1823). The coset theory is Gauss, DA arts. 312-318 (1801).

results.what: Reduction to e = phi(N)/ord_N(10) periods; multiplication of the numerator by 10 rotates the period
results.modern_name: Coset decomposition of (Z/N)^* by the subgroup generated by 10
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), art. 314ff; the table itself was published posthumously in Werke II (1863)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working sheet for Gauss's known table of decimal periods (announced in DA art. 316, printed in Werke II). The computations are correct, routine and already attributed to him. The only minor details are his self-corrections and the start-at-smallest-numerator-above-N/10 convention.
